text: [excited] You wake up. And something is very, very different. [curious] You can hear the fridge downstairs. You can hear your own heartbeat. You can count the threads in your blanket. [whisper] Last night, you took a tiny pill from a very suspicious website. And now… your brain is switching on. All of it. [tense] Movies love this idea. Use a hundred percent of your brain, become a genius. But at a hundred percent, something happens that no movie ever shows you. [sarcastic] Don't worry. We'll get there. Probably.

[curious] First, let's look inside. This is your brain. A city of eighty-six billion neurons. Every neuron is a tiny worker passing sparks to its neighbours. That's a thought. Sparks, passed along. Billions of times a second. [playful] This is Neil. Neil is a neuron. Neil has worked here since before you were born. Neil is tired. [curious] And here's the weird part. On a normal day, most of the city is dark. Only small groups of lights switch on at any moment. A district for seeing. A district for remembering. A district for being scared of spiders. [tense] But not today. Today, the whole city is waking up.

[excited] Twenty-five percent. You walk downstairs, and you notice… everything. Every word on the cereal box. Every crack in the ceiling. The exact moment the toast is about to pop. [curious] And this part is real. Your eyes send your brain millions of bits of information every second. But scientists estimate you only consciously notice a tiny trickle of it. Your brain throws the rest away so you don't go mad. [deadpan] Today, your brain stopped throwing it away. [curious] And here's something you've never noticed. There's a hole in your vision right now. Every eye has a blind spot, where the nerve leaves the eye. Your brain simply paints over it. Today, you can see the hole. [playful] You also remember where you left everything. The TV remote. Your first tooth. Every password you've ever forgotten. [sarcastic] Your cat is staring at you. Your cat is not impressed.

[building] Fifty percent. You open a book. You finish the book. It took forty seconds. There was a real man named Kim Peek who could read two pages at once. One with each eye. He remembered almost everything he read. [excited] By lunch, you've learned to juggle, speak Italian, and play the piano. Badly, then brilliantly. [deadpan] There's just one problem. You are starving. [curious] Because your brain is greedy. It's only about two percent of your body weight, but it burns about twenty percent of your energy. Running on roughly twenty watts. About the same as a dim light bulb. [sarcastic] At fifty percent, you've eaten nine sandwiches. Neil has started a union.

[excited] Seventy-five percent. Now you start seeing patterns everywhere. You know what people will say before they say it. You finish the waiter's sentence. You finish his next sentence too. He leaves. [building] In the park, a chess champion is beating everyone. You beat him in four moves. Without looking. [deadpan] A pigeon lands next to you. You calculate its flight path, its mood, and what it had for lunch. [tense] But the patterns don't switch off. You see faces in the clouds. Faces in the toast. Your socks are judging you. [curious] That's real too. It's called pareidolia. Your brain is so hungry for patterns, especially faces, that it finds them where there aren't any. Everyone does it. Today, you can't stop. [playful] Actually, quick question. How many faces did you just see in this room? Tell us in the comments.

[sarcastic] And now, at this point, someone in the comments is typing: "Actually, we use a hundred percent of our brain already." [deadpan] And annoyingly… they're right. [curious] The "ten percent" idea is a myth. Nobody knows exactly where it started, but brain scans show that over a normal day, you use pretty much all of your brain. Every district does a job. The difference is, you never use it all at the same time. At any moment, only a small slice of your neurons are firing. That's not laziness. That's the design. [tense] But today, the districts aren't taking turns. They're all staying on.

[building] Ninety percent. Someone books you on live TV. The biggest quiz show in the country. [excited] You answer every question before the host finishes reading it. Capital of Mongolia. Ulaanbaatar. The atomic number of gold. Seventy-nine. What the host had for breakfast. Eggs. He's furious. [building] The audience is chanting your name. Your mum is texting you in all capitals. [tense] But inside your head, the city is on fire. Every memory is playing at once. Every song you've ever heard is stuck in your head at the same time. [urgent] Neil is running. Neil has never run. [tense] Final question. For one million.

[whisper] One hundred percent. [quiet] And this is the part the movies never show you. [tense] When every neuron fires at once, it isn't genius. It's a power cut. [curious] In real life, when huge groups of neurons fire together all at once, that's what a seizure is. The brain's signals stop making sense, because nothing is taking turns anymore. [warm] Seizures are a real medical condition that lots of people live with, and doctors can really help. But they show the big secret of your brain. It works because it doesn't switch everything on.

[quiet] You wake up on the studio floor. The whole country just watched. [warm] The pill has worn off. You're back to normal. Which, it turns out, was a hundred percent all along. [deadpan] You did not win the million. But you can still speak Italian. Mostly. [playful] At home, the cat is asleep. The cat has been using its brain perfectly all day.

[warm] So here's the truth. Your brain isn't lazy. It isn't ten percent. It's an eighty-six-billion-worker city that knows exactly when to rest. [playful] If you could switch on one district to a hundred percent, just for a day, which one would you pick? Comments. [sarcastic] And Neil, take the day off. You've earned it.
